studies.caveats: observational design, single-center
studies.fact_check_note: The study covers all eligible Irish acute hospitals so 'single-center' is not applicable; caveat removed. No industry funding declared.

ideas.title: Is it real? Testosterone fuels prostate cancer
ideas.angle: Online TRT clinics and 'low T' content often dismiss the cancer fear as a myth, and many doctors still repeat it. A pooled analysis of 24,510 men across 10 cohorts, with testosterone measured by mass spectrometry, found no link between higher natural testosterone and cancer death, overall cancer or prostate cancer. The catch is the receipt: natural levels aren't therapy, so the study can't settle whether TRT is safe.
ideas.why_now: Testosterone therapy marketing to men, and increasingly to women, is a steady viral wellness claim. TFM has no age limit, and this is a high-quality data source for a 'yes, but' verdict.
ideas.is_it_real: Strong design: individual participant data from 10 prospective cohorts, 276,931 person-years, at least 5 years of follow-up. It's still observational, and it covers endogenous hormone levels, not supplementation. The digest says the abstract was cut off mid-results, so read the full paper and confirm the exact null results before writing. The 'tiny sample' flag is a parsing error.

studies.headline: Higher testosterone levels in older men are not linked to greater cancer risk, large study finds
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: The abstract was truncated in the source data at the findings section; summary reflects available findings. The N=24,510 and study design details are confirmed from the methods section. The direction of effect (no significant association with cancer risk) is stated in context from the background framing; journalists should verify the full published findings.

ideas.title: Over a decade with Parkinson's, psychosis and apathy climbed while anxiety eased
ideas.angle: In 846 people with biomarker-confirmed Parkinson's tracked for 10 years, the odds of psychosis rose about 21% per year and apathy about 17% per year, while anxiety dipped slightly. It's a useful heads-up for families on what to watch for as the disease progresses.
ideas.why_now: Trend Desk has Marshall Faulk's Parkinson's disclosure as a roundup item this week, so this could run next to it. The study has been online 19 days (verified).
ideas.is_it_real: A large, well-characterized cohort (PPMI), but observational. The effects are per-year odds ratios, not prevalence. The digest's 'psychosis nearly doubled' line isn't backed by the summary, so don't use it. The digest calls PPMI US-only, but it has international sites, so check before saying so.

studies.headline: Psychosis and apathy — not anxiety — emerge as the fastest-growing psychiatric burdens in Parkinson's disease over a decade
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (US) cohort

ideas.title: An ER visit for a fall can be an early warning sign of a first seizure
ideas.angle: Across 57,547 adults with a first seizure in 11 states, the odds of a fall-related ER visit in the week before the seizure were about 2.6 times the odds in the same week a year earlier. The signal stretched back as far as 22 weeks. Unexplained falls deserve a second look.
ideas.why_now: Recent (about 10 days, date unverified; confirm it's within the 21-day roundup window). It's a practical, quick takeaway for readers and caregivers.
ideas.is_it_real: A case-crossover design using administrative ER data. That's a reasonable method, but the figure is an odds ratio, not 'times more likely', and it only covers the 7,307 people who had a prior fall visit. Mean age was 49, so it's not an older-adult finding. Some 'falls' may have been unrecognized seizures, which supports the point rather than undermining it.

studies.headline: Falls before a first seizure aren't just accidents — ER data suggest they're missed warning signs
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, no age breakdown reported, mean age 49.3 years (older adult subgroup not separately analyzed)

ideas.title: Six minutes of daily stretching eased fibromyalgia symptoms in a small six-week trial
ideas.angle: A useful, quick number. A home routine short enough to actually do improved fibromyalgia impact scores by about 19%, and adherence was 83%. That's relevant for a condition where high-intensity exercise often backfires.
ideas.why_now: Online about 17 days (unverified). It's an RCT with a takeaway readers can use.
ideas.is_it_real: Small RCT: 58 adults, six weeks, compared against a waitlist rather than a placebo or attention control, with self-reported outcomes. The authors flag a sex imbalance. The caveat clause: small, short, and unblinded. Confirm the online date before it runs.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), short follow-up, waitlist-controlled (not placebo-controlled), self-reported outcomes, sex imbalance noted by authors

ideas.title: Cancer cachexia: the wasting most patients are never told about, and the mealtime fights it causes at home
ideas.beat: aging, body and metabolism: cancer and caregiving
ideas.angle: Three papers from two journals agree that cachexia is rarely discussed in clinic. Families end up working it out from contradictory websites, and the worst suffering is emotional: guilt, anxiety and conflict over food. The Western diagnostic criteria may miss that distress entirely. A caregiving feature on 'feeding someone who can't eat', not a drug story.
ideas.why_now: Online 54 to 58 days ago. Per the digest's score note, this matches an interest Meagan saved on cancer cachexia communication gaps. The pitch agents should check where Pfizer's ponsegromab (GDF-15 antibody) program stands now. If there's a late-stage readout, that is the stronger hook, but don't assert one without confirming it.
ideas.is_it_real: The evidence is thin, which fits a feature built on experience but not a news claim. The only original data is a survey of 192 advanced-cancer patients in Japan and South Korea: Asian (AWGC) criteria tracked eating-related distress and the European (EPCRC) criteria did not. Self-reported and cross-sectional. The other two are a narrative review from Edinburgh and Marie Curie and a single advocate's perspective piece with no primary data. No prevalence or survival numbers should come from these papers.

studies.headline: A newer Asian cachexia definition captures more eating-related suffering in cancer patients than the European standard
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, study population limited to Japan and South Korea (generalizability to Western populations uncertain), no age breakdown reported, no age range specified beyond 'adult'
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract does not report a specific age range for the 192 participants beyond 'adult patients'; 'no age breakdown reported' caveat applied accordingly.

ideas.title: Does virtual pelvic floor therapy work for bladder leaks? What 13 trials show
ideas.beat: women's health: menopause and pelvic health
ideas.angle: An evergreen page for women with stress urinary incontinence who can't get to a pelvic floor PT. Pelvic floor training delivered by app or video reduced symptoms and improved quality of life, and it did about as well as in-person physiotherapy, not better.
ideas.why_now: Searches for bladder leakage and pelvic floor therapy are steady. An evergreen page needs solid evidence, and this review has it.

ideas.title: Is it real? Barefoot shoes prevent running injuries
ideas.beat: viral health and wellness claims: fitness gear
ideas.angle: In nearly 4,800 runners, injury rates were the same in minimalist and regular shoes. The runners who stuck with barefoot shoes reported fewer injuries, but most people who tried them quit, which is a textbook survivor-bias setup. A good receipt for 'the shoe isn't the fix, the transition is'.
ideas.why_now: Barefoot and minimalist shoes are a steady wellness-gear trend. The claim is not in this week's search list, so this is a backlog post, not a timely one.
ideas.is_it_real: An online survey of 4,719 Brazilian runners: self-reported, cross-sectional, one country. Overall injury rates did not differ. Habitual users had lower odds of injury (OR 0.72), but that's an odds ratio, not '28% less likely'. And people who got hurt probably switched back, so the habitual-user benefit may be survivorship. The post would need the randomized transition trials as well; this study is one receipt.

studies.headline: Runners who stick with minimalist shoes long-term have lower injury odds — but most people who try them quit
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, elite athlete sample (may not generalize — Brazilian running community context)

ideas.title: Is it real? Weighted blankets help you sleep
ideas.beat: viral health and wellness claims: sleep
ideas.angle: Meagan saved this. In a rigorous but tiny crossover trial in a dementia unit, weighted blankets did not measurably improve sleep, though falls and restraint use were lower during blanket weeks. That gives a 'not what the marketing says, but not nothing' frame for a claim everyone repeats.
ideas.why_now: Weighted blankets stay a perennial sleep-gadget claim, and Meagan saved this study on the dashboard.
ideas.is_it_real: A pilot with only 14 residents with behavioral symptoms of dementia, at one Australian unit, two weeks per condition. Compliance varied, and the authors say their actigraphy device couldn't measure sleep properly. The falls and restraint signal is descriptive, not statistically tested. It can't speak to healthy adults or insomnia, so the post would need the trials in those populations. On its own it can't carry the post.

studies.headline: Weighted blankets don't improve sleep in dementia patients — but fewer falls and less use of restraints occurred during use
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, variable protocol compliance, actigraphy device inadequate for sleep measurement, pilot study only, industry funding [Dementia Australia — research grant funder]

ideas.title: Does OsteoStrong work? A randomized trial says the 20-minute bone machine builds strength but loses to real exercise on balance
ideas.angle: An evergreen 'does OsteoStrong work' page for women past menopause with osteopenia or osteoporosis. In the BONEMORE trial, once-weekly OsteoStrong matched a twice-weekly 60-minute exercise program on grip strength, back strength and sit-to-stand. The exercise program beat it on gait speed, trunk extension endurance and one-leg balance, which are the outcomes most tied to falls.
ideas.why_now: OsteoStrong is a franchise with steady branded search, and readers comparing it with a gym program want a randomized answer. An evergreen page doesn't need a news peg.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a randomized trial (n=194, women 65-79, Karolinska, 9 months), which is unusual for a commercial gym concept. These are secondary outcomes, so the page should check whether the primary bone-density results were published separately and what they showed. The trial ran at one center in Sweden and did not measure fractures or falls, only strength and balance tests. Its participants are older than the site's core 40-65 reader, so frame it as 'the decade after' or for readers' mothers.

studies.headline: A trendy bone-loading machine improves strength in older women with osteoporosis — but traditional exercise still wins on balance and gait
studies.caveats: single-center, women only, Swedish population (Karolinska Institutet), secondary outcomes analysis, short follow-up (9 months)

ideas.title: Is it real? Rainy weather makes your joints act up
ideas.angle: Test the old belief that your knees can forecast rain. In 14 years of Madrid primary-care records covering 1,175 people with rheumatoid arthritis or axial spondyloarthritis, more rain was linked to fewer RA doctor visits, not more. Longer sunshine was linked to fewer visits for spondyloarthritis. This study is one receipt among several, not the whole post.
ideas.why_now: The clocks fall back Nov 1 and cold, wet weather is starting, which is when the joint-forecast claim comes back every year. The study went online about 40 days ago (date verified).
ideas.is_it_real: The study is observational and measured how often patients saw a doctor, not how much pain they had. Fewer visits on rainy days could simply mean people stay home when it rains. It covers three clinics in one city, and 73% of patients were women. The post needs other receipts: the UK smartphone study 'Cloudy with a Chance of Pain' (Dixon et al., 2019) found a small link between pain and humidity or pressure, and a 2017 BMJ analysis of Medicare visits found no link with rainfall. Both should be confirmed before use. The likely honest answer is 'maybe a little for some people, but not enough to send you to the doctor'.

studies.headline: Bad weather doesn't drive arthritis patients to the doctor — and sunshine might keep spondyloarthritis patients away
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center region (Madrid, Spain), consultation frequency may not reflect disease activity, secondary analysis of health records, study population predominantly female (73%)

ideas.title: Sports science is finally studying women, and the findings don't fit the advice built on men
ideas.angle: Four recent studies from four journals look at women's bodies on their own terms. Across 1.35 million ultramarathon finishes, women slowed less than men as heat and humidity rose. A meta-analysis covering more than 18 million people found no clear sign that the pill prevents ACL tears. In 24 women, how much estrogen swung from day to day tracked with sprint power better than cycle phase did. Teen girls who wore men's cleats reported about twice the odds of injury. Taken together they make a service explainer about what female athletes have been told and what the newer evidence says.
ideas.why_now: The hormone-variability study (JSCR) went online 16 days ago, so the piece can call it the latest. ACL tears in women's soccer are still a live sports-health story, and two of these studies speak to it directly: birth control and cleat design.
ideas.is_it_real: The evidence is mixed in strength. The ultramarathon study is huge, but it uses race results only, with no physiology, so it can't say why women hold up better in heat. The ACL meta-analysis is a null result (pooled RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01) with very high heterogeneity (I²=97%). Its online date is unverified, so the writer should frame it as 'doesn't show protection', not 'proves no effect'. The hormone study had 24 women and is observational. The cleats study is a retrospective self-report survey of 99 girls, and its odds ratio must not be written as 'twice as likely'. The piece should present this as an emerging picture, not settled science.

ideas.title: $200+ smart swim goggles didn't make swimmers any faster than the same workouts without them
ideas.angle: In a 12-week randomized trial of 57 recreational swimmers, real-time-feedback goggles (FORM) did no better than following the same training plan without them. Both groups improved swim speed by about 6–7%. The plan did the work, not the gadget.

ideas.title: Cleared to play isn't the same as healed: new ACL studies show the return-to-sport checklist misses re-tear and arthritis risk
ideas.angle: A feature on what the standard ACL recovery benchmarks miss. In pro athletes, the limb-symmetry hop test barely separated those who later re-tore their graft from those who didn't. Patients who got their quad strength back still walked abnormally a year after surgery. A knee that couldn't fully straighten at two months, and shifted joint loading, both tracked with early cartilage loss. An 18-year-old with a steep tibial slope had about a 37% modeled chance of graft rupture. Taller men with thin hamstring grafts had more revisions. In one cohort, return-to-sport rates looked similar with or without surgery. Parents of teen athletes are the readers.
ideas.why_now: Several of these studies came out in the last 45 to 50 days, and the fall high school and college sports season is when ACL tears pile up.
ideas.is_it_real: Most of these are small, single-center or observational: the gait and cartilage studies have 30 to 59 patients, and the re-tear test study has 64 cases and controls drawn from 127 elite athletes. The 37% figure is a modeled probability from one retrospective hamstring-graft cohort, and it was flagged as a subgroup finding. The surgery-vs-no-surgery comparison wasn't randomized, so patients chose their treatment, and that study's online date is unverified. The strongest pieces are a 9,448-player Swedish registry and a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs on graft choice that only goes out to 24 months. Together they show the gaps are real, not how to close them.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, industry funding [Arthritis Foundation — non-industry but noted], observational design

studies.headline: Most ACL patients return to sport whether or not they have surgery — but high-demand sport athletes take a year longer
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes

studies.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
studies.headline: Failing to fully straighten your knee two months after ACL surgery may quietly accelerate cartilage breakdown
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, observational design

studies.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
studies.headline: ACL reconstruction shifts where your knee absorbs pressure during walking — and that shift may quietly erode cartilage for years
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, cadaveric biomechanical component (not living tissue), short follow-up for OA outcomes, study population in China

studies.headline: Taller Football Players With Smaller ACL Grafts Face Nearly Triple the Revision Risk
studies.caveats: observational design, retrospective cohort study, elite athlete sample (may not generalize), single sport (football/soccer)

studies.headline: A Less-Used ACL Graft Matches the Gold Standard in Outcomes — With Fewer Side Effects
studies.caveats: short follow-up (evidence only to 24 months), moderate GRADE certainty for most outcomes, heterogeneity across trials

ideas.title: Is it real? Collagen supplements make your skin look younger
ideas.angle: Collagen keeps reinventing itself (powders, gummies, now 'tripeptides'). This systematic review of 25 RCTs found that most trials reported better skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles than placebo. It also rated most of those trials at high risk of bias. The post can say the results look good on paper and explain why the paper is thin.
ideas.why_now: Trend Desk shows 'collagen tripeptides' exploding this week. That pairing makes this the receipt for the 'Is it real?' question.
ideas.is_it_real: The review covered 25 randomized trials of 13 to 236 people, mostly healthy volunteers. Positive results: 10 of 15 trials on hydration, 10 of 13 on elasticity, 9 of 10 on wrinkles. The authors rated most trials at high risk of bias, and trials were short. It tested hydrolyzed collagen in general, not tripeptides specifically, so it can't settle the newer product claim. One author works for a life sciences consultancy.

studies.headline: Collagen supplements may improve skin elasticity and hydration, but most supporting trials have serious quality problems
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), high risk of bias in most included trials, short follow-up, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: Sample size range (13–236), number of included RCTs (25), and breakdown of positive findings by outcome (hydration 10/15, elasticity 10/13, wrinkles 9/10) verified against abstract. High risk of bias rating confirmed. One author (M.S.) disclosed employment by Lumanity, a life sciences consultancy, though no direct conflict of interest specific to the review was declared.

ideas.title: Is it real? You should sync your workouts to your menstrual cycle
ideas.beat: viral health and wellness claims / the body
ideas.angle: Cycle syncing tells women to plan training around cycle phases. In 42 elite soccer players, naturally cycling women had moderately lower quad strength during their period days, and women on hormonal birth control showed no dip. That's a real but narrow effect, far from the full phase-by-phase plans sold online.
ideas.why_now: Cycle syncing is a long-running social media fitness claim, and receipts for it are rare. This study is old enough that only tfm fits.
ideas.is_it_real: Small: 21 naturally cycling and 21 hormonal contraceptive users, all elite athletes, tested over one 40-day preseason. Cycle phase was estimated from apps and calendars, not confirmed with hormone tests. It measured strength in the lab, not training results. It supports a modest strength dip in the early follicular phase only. It says nothing about the luteal-phase or diet parts of cycle syncing.

studies.journal: Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport
studies.headline: Elite female soccer players are measurably weaker in the first week of their menstrual cycle — but hormonal contraceptive users show no such dip
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), elite athlete sample (may not generalize), cycle phases estimated via app/calendar (not hormone verification), short follow-up

ideas.title: Does canned food have BPA? An 18,000-person survey links canned food, instant noodles and burgers to higher levels
ideas.angle: An evergreen food-safety explainer on BPA in canned and packaged food. Adults who ate canned foods, instant noodles and burgers often had higher urinary BPA. National levels fell after South Korea tightened its food-contact rules, which gives the page a 'regulation works' section.
ideas.why_now: There is steady search demand for BPA and canned food, and the chemical-avoidance trend is still running (Trend Desk shows 'non-toxic air fryer' emerging).
ideas.is_it_real: This is a large national survey across four cycles from 2009 to 2020, but it is observational: food intake was self-reported and BPA was measured in urine at one point in time. It's Korean data, and diets and regulations differ from the US. It shows higher exposure, not health harm. It matches long-standing evidence that canned food raises BPA levels.

studies.headline: Canned foods, instant noodles, and burgers linked to higher BPA levels in the body, large Korean survey finds
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (South Korea — dietary and regulatory patterns may not generalize directly to US or global populations), self-reported food consumption

ideas.title: Fatty liver finally has drugs. New research says the bigger story is timing: when the weight came, whether you cut back drinking, even sugar in infancy
ideas.angle: A explainer-feature on MASLD, the liver disease estimated to affect about a third of adults. Semaglutide and resmetirom are now approved for its severe form, and recent cohorts are changing the prevention advice: cutting back on alcohol, even unevenly, was linked to fewer serious liver outcomes; the 'obesity paradox' mostly disappears once you account for when people gained weight; and people exposed to WWII sugar rationing in their first 1,000 days had less liver disease decades later.
ideas.why_now: Semaglutide's 2025 approval for MASH moved fatty liver into the GLP-1 conversation. The lead study is 37 days old (verified), and holiday drinking season plus 'cut back, don't quit' drinking trends give the alcohol finding a consumer hook.
ideas.is_it_real: All three primary studies are observational. Alcohol (AJG, 85,554 Koreans with MetALD, median 10 years): adjusted HR 0.80 for fluctuating and 0.70 for consistently reduced drinking vs sustained drinking. These are relative risks only; the absolute event rates still need pulling, and the result covers people who already had MetALD. Obesity paradox (CGH, NHANES plus UK Biobank): persistent adult obesity HR 1.79 and rapid BMI gain HR 1.93 for death. Its online date is unverified (47 days per the digest). Sugar rationing (CGH, 63,698 UK Biobank): a natural experiment where exposure is assigned by birth year, not by measured intake; about 30% lower MASLD risk. Online date unverified, about 78 days. The Gut and Liver piece is a narrative review that supplies the treatment landscape. Say 'linked to' throughout.
ideas.other_peg: Wegovy/semaglutide FDA approval for MASH with fibrosis in 2025 (confirm date); holiday drinking season

studies.headline: Even Cutting Back Alcohol Inconsistently Lowers Liver Disease Risk — You Don't Have to Quit Completely
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (South Korea), self-reported alcohol intake implied by screening data, no causation established

studies.headline: The 'obesity paradox' in fatty liver disease is a statistical illusion — timing of weight gain is what actually predicts survival
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake possible in NHANES, secondary analysis of existing cohorts

studies.headline: Cutting sugar in the first two years of life is linked to dramatically lower liver disease risk decades later
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, exposure defined by birth year relative to policy (not individually measured sugar intake), findings tied to a specific UK historical context

studies.headline: FDA-approved drugs like Ozempic are reshaping fatty liver disease treatment — and a wave of new therapies is right behind them
studies.caveats: review article (no primary data), short follow-up data cited for some agents

ideas.title: WIC, the food program that already limits what families can buy, is linked to better toddler diets than SNAP, just as states start banning soda from SNAP
ideas.angle: States, Nebraska reportedly first, are getting USDA waivers to restrict soda and candy purchases with SNAP. WIC has always worked that way, with a prescribed food package. A national study following 3,051 WIC-enrolled children from birth to age 5 found that steady WIC participation tracked with better diet quality, while children in SNAP households scored lower. Separate NHANES data show kids' sugary-drink intake had already nearly halved before any bans.
ideas.why_now: SNAP food-restriction waivers and SNAP benefit changes from the 2025 budget law are rolling out now. Trend Desk shows 'supplemental nutrition assistance program' as an emerging search. There's a Midwest and Omaha angle as well.
ideas.is_it_real: Both studies are observational. In the WIC ITFPS-2 study, SNAP households likely differ in income and stress, so this does not show SNAP worsens diets. Healthy Eating Index scores come from parent-reported recalls, and infant diet quality explained up to 30% of the SNAP gap. The soda-trend study (youth SSB drinkers 76% to 44%, 2003–2023) is by Exponent, a consultancy with beverage-industry clients, and its result suits that interest; disclose it. Pitch agents must confirm which states have waivers and their effective dates. The study is 40 days old, so it needs the policy peg.
ideas.other_peg: USDA SNAP soda/candy restriction waivers taking effect in 2026 (Nebraska among the first; confirm), plus SNAP changes under the 2025 budget law

studies.headline: WIC participation predicts better diets in toddlers, but SNAP enrollment is linked to lower diet quality — even in infancy
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, secondary analysis

studies.headline: Americans Have Quietly Cut Their Soda Habit Nearly in Half Over Two Decades — But the Drop May Slow
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, industry funding [Exponent Inc., a consulting firm with food and beverage industry clients]

ideas.title: Is it real? 'Nature's Ozempic': can resistant starch, fiber or berberine stand in for a GLP-1 drug, or hold the weight off after you stop?
ideas.angle: Two reviews give the receipts. One finds that slowly digested and resistant starches can nudge the body's own GLP-1 release, but only in mechanistic data. The other looked for supplements to use after quitting a GLP-1 drug and found no direct evidence in people who have stopped. Answer: there's a real mechanism, the dose is nowhere near a drug's, and the post-GLP-1 supplement claims are untested.
ideas.why_now: Trend Desk shows 'managing weight loss after glp-1' exploding. 'Nature's Ozempic' marketing for berberine and fiber products is still widespread.
ideas.is_it_real: Neither paper is new human data. The starch paper is a mechanistic literature review; the GLP-1 drug comparison is the digest's framing, not the authors'. The supplement paper is a single-author narrative review from 'The B Fueled Foundation' (no conflicts declared, but the affiliation is worth checking). It extrapolates from meta-analyses in people who never took GLP-1 drugs, and the author says so. The thin evidence is the finding. The claim that nearly half of users quit within a year is the review's own; check the source.

studies.headline: Nearly half of GLP-1 users quit within a year — could fiber and berberine help fill the gap?
studies.caveats: observational design, small sample (N<100), self-reported dietary intake, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: The review is by a single author affiliated with 'The B Fueled Foundation,' an affiliation that warrants scrutiny for potential conflicts of interest, though none are declared. Evidence is extrapolated from non-GLP-1RA populations — the abstract itself acknowledges this limitation explicitly.

studies.journal: Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition
studies.headline: Resistant starch may trigger the same gut hormone that powers Ozempic — without the injection
studies.caveats: review article not original research, no primary human data collected, microbiome data only (no clinical outcomes), mechanistic framework not yet clinically validated
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract does not report an N or a study population because this is a review, not a trial. The GLP-1 drug parallel is implied by the science but not explicitly stated in the abstract — this framing is the writer's interpretation and should be clearly attributed as context, not a direct finding of the paper.

ideas.title: Is it real? Pair vitamin C with iron-rich food so you absorb more iron
ideas.angle: The squeeze-lemon-on-your-spinach rule, tested in a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs. Eating vitamin C-rich fruit with meals did raise ferritin and hemoglobin, but measured iron absorption, the reason everyone gives, barely moved. The advice works for iron stores; the textbook explanation is shakier.
ideas.why_now: Iron and ferritin are a steady wellness-TikTok topic. This tests the most repeated pairing rule. It is distinct from the ferritin-cutoff pitch already filed.
ideas.is_it_real: A systematic review of 15 RCTs (N=1,381, mostly females aged 15–74 plus children). Blood-marker gains were rated moderate certainty; the absorption result is low certainty. 'No significant effect' on absorption is not proof of no effect. The fruits and juices tested varied. About 122 days old, so it works for tfm only.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.headline: Eating vitamin C-rich fruit with meals raises iron markers in the blood—but may not actually boost how much iron your gut absorbs
studies.caveats: None identified

ideas.title: Your afternoon snack was linked to a bigger blood-sugar bump than a morning one, and moving for half an hour afterward blunted it
ideas.angle: 785 adults without diabetes wore glucose monitors and activity trackers for nine days. Afternoon and early-evening snacks produced larger glucose rises than morning ones, even after accounting for what was eaten, and moderate-to-vigorous activity in the 30 minutes after was linked to smaller rises. A useful line for the glucose-spike crowd.
ideas.why_now: Online 18 days (verified), and CGMs for people without diabetes are a live wellness trend.
ideas.is_it_real: Observational, Singapore only, self-reported food. The outcome is two-hour glucose area under the curve, not health outcomes. Nobody has shown that snack-level glucose bumps matter for people without diabetes.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.headline: Afternoon snacking spikes blood sugar more than morning snacking — even if you eat the exact same thing
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country cohort (Singapore), self-reported dietary intake, no clinical outcomes beyond glucose iAUC

ideas.title: A Mediterranean lifestyle was linked to 30% lower death risk across every income and education level, and higher earners saw the biggest gap
ideas.angle: 105,812 Dutch adults followed for 13 years. The highest adherence to a Mediterranean diet-plus-lifestyle score (food, activity, rest, social habits) was linked to 30% lower all-cause mortality. Income amplified the association more than education did, which is a quiet hint that money matters more than knowing what to eat.
ideas.why_now: Online 16 days (verified). The disparity angle is the twist on a familiar diet story.
ideas.is_it_real: Observational. Self-reported diet scored once at baseline, Dutch cohort. HR 0.70 is a relative figure. The 46%-lower figure for high income plus high adherence compares against a reference group that mixes income and adherence, so frame the income point as suggestive.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.headline: A Mediterranean lifestyle cuts mortality risk by 30% regardless of education — but income amplifies the benefit far more than schooling does
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, Dutch cohort (may not generalize globally), MEDLIFE scored at baseline only

ideas.title: ARFID isn't just picky eating: across 84 studies, about 44% of kids with it also had an anxiety disorder and nearly a third had nutritional deficiencies
ideas.angle: A meta-analysis putting numbers on how medically and psychiatrically tangled the 'picky eating disorder' is. GI disorders in 30%, nutritional deficiencies in 32%, anxiety in 44%, autism in 19%. Useful for parents who've seen ARFID on TikTok.
ideas.why_now: Online 21 days (verified, the last day roundup-eligible). ARFID awareness keeps rising online.
ideas.is_it_real: Pooled prevalence from mostly clinical samples, which skew toward sicker kids. Heterogeneity is high, publication bias was detected, and GRADE certainty is very low to low. Present the figures as rough estimates.

studies.headline: Nearly half of children with ARFID have an anxiety disorder — and almost a third have nutritional deficiencies, large meta-analysis finds
studies.caveats: observational design, high heterogeneity (I²≥75%), publication bias detected for anxiety/depression/nutritional deficiencies, very low to low GRADE certainty of evidence

ideas.title: Childhood abuse was linked to chronic constipation decades later in a large Harvard-affiliated cohort
ideas.angle: A gut-brain item. Gastroenterology adds chronic constipation to the list of gut conditions tied to early-life adversity, which suggests some stubborn constipation may not be a fiber problem.
ideas.why_now: Online 17 days (verified), in a top GI journal, and not widely covered.
ideas.is_it_real: The digest worked from the title and affiliations only; the abstract wasn't available. Before this runs, pull the paper for the cohort name, N and the odds ratio, and report it as an odds ratio. Abuse history is self-reported and recalled, and the design is observational. If the effect is small, cut it.

studies.headline: Childhood abuse leaves a lasting mark on the gut — raising chronic constipation risk decades later
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported dietary intake, self-reported abuse history, no mechanistic data, sample size not confirmed in abstract
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was not fully available — summary based on title, author affiliations, and journal context. Sample size (N) could not be verified from the available text.

ideas.title: Probiotics for menopause: what the 'estrobolome' research does and doesn't show
ideas.angle: An evergreen explainer on the gut-menopause axis. Falling estrogen shifts gut bacteria, and some gut bacteria recycle estrogen. It covers what probiotic and prebiotic trials show for bone, metabolism and hot flashes, and where the evidence is thin.
ideas.why_now: Steady search demand for menopause probiotics and estrobolome supplements. The review gives a current map of the evidence.
ideas.is_it_real: A bibliometric and narrative review, not new data. The underlying trials are mostly small and short; bone health has the most evidence. The page should say no probiotic is proven to treat menopause symptoms.

studies.headline: Gut bacteria may be a hidden driver of menopause symptoms — and probiotics could help rebalance the system
studies.caveats: observational design, no original human data, narrative review methodology subject to selection bias, microbiome data only (no clinical outcomes from primary study), short follow-up in underlying trials

ideas.title: After a young person's first self-harm ER visit, the next month is the riskiest, and the visit itself can flag abuse or a substance problem
ideas.beat: women's health and the mind (youth mental health)
ideas.angle: A parent-facing explainer: three big registry studies from three countries suggest a first self-harm visit should be treated as a signal, not a one-off. The first 30 days are when repeat attempts cluster. Self-harm also predicts later presentations for sexual abuse, and substance use disorders carry the highest self-harm risk of any diagnosis. So follow-up needs to cover safety and substance use, and go beyond a short stabilization.
ideas.why_now: The Hong Kong study is the newest piece (17 days, date unverified). Together the three answer the question parents ask after an ER visit: what happens next, and what should we watch for.
ideas.is_it_real: These are all observational registry studies, but large ones. Sweden: 77,647 young people aged 10–24 followed from their first hospital-treated self-harm (1973–2019). In the first month, 8.4% self-harmed again and 2.9% attempted suicide. Males had the highest suicide risk and 10–12-year-olds the highest first-month risk. Ontario: 139,233 children and teens (2013–2022). The 10-year cumulative incidence of a sexual-abuse presentation was 9.06% versus 1.26% in matched controls (HR 8.32, falling to 5.06 after adjustment). That is a marker of vulnerability, not proof self-harm leads to abuse. Hong Kong: 322,922 people with a first mental health diagnosis, all ages. Self-harm HR was 10.59 for any disorder and 22.86 for substance use disorders, highest at age 24 and under. Hazard ratios are not 'times more likely' in plain terms. Health records miss self-harm that never reaches a hospital. The Swedish data reach back to 1973, so current care may differ. Handle carefully and follow suicide-reporting guidelines.

studies.headline: Across every mental health diagnosis, self-harm risk is dramatically elevated — but substance use disorders top the list by a wide margin
studies.caveats: observational design, single-region sample (Hong Kong), health-record data may miss undetected self-harm, WEIRD sample caveat partially offset by large non-Western population

studies.headline: The month after a young person's first self-harm hospitalization is the most dangerous — and most overlooked — window for suicide risk
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

studies.headline: Children who self-harm are eight times more likely to later present for sexual abuse — a finding that reframes self-harm as a vulnerability marker
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis

ideas.title: Can't name what you feel? That's linked to compulsive scrolling, and the link is stronger in adults than teens
ideas.beat: women's health and the mind / internet culture
ideas.angle: The social media debate is about teens and depression. A preregistered meta-analysis of 83 studies finds that alexithymia (trouble identifying and describing your own emotions) tracks with problematic social media, gaming and phone use even after accounting for depression and anxiety. The link is stronger in adults than adolescents. The pitch reframes doomscrolling as a stand-in for emotions you can't read, not a willpower failure.
ideas.why_now: Online 14 days (verified), not widely covered. It cuts against a teen-centered phone panic that is still running.
ideas.is_it_real: It's a meta-analysis of 83 studies and 42,478 people, preregistered, with a pooled correlation of r = 0.36. That is moderate, not large. The included studies are observational and mostly cross-sectional, and outcomes are self-reported, so direction is unknown: heavy scrolling could blunt emotional awareness just as easily as the reverse. Say 'linked to', never 'drives'. Samples skew Western and educated.

studies.headline: People who can't identify their own emotions are significantly more likely to develop problematic internet and social media use
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, WEIRD sample (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic)

ideas.title: Researchers turned 991 Soft White Underbelly interviews into an addiction study, with AI helping do the coding
ideas.beat: internet culture / health AI / public health
ideas.angle: A viral, much-criticized YouTube interview series has become a research dataset. Researchers coded 3.9 million words of first-person addiction stories with help from a large language model. They found that people who want to recover keep hitting structural walls: no ID, stigma, system access. The story has two layers: what the stories show about recovery, and whether a commercial channel accused of exploiting its subjects should be science's data source.
ideas.why_now: Online 25 days (verified), not widely covered. Health AI and creator-economy ethics are both live.
ideas.is_it_real: This is qualitative work on a non-representative sample: people a YouTube channel chose to film, paid, and edited for an audience. The coding was LLM-assisted, a new method with unclear reliability. The eight-stage model is descriptive, and the 'structural barriers' finding echoes much earlier research. The novelty is the method and source, not the conclusion. Pitch agents should check how the authors handled consent and the channel's editing.

studies.headline: Nearly 1,000 firsthand addiction narratives reveal that structural barriers — not just motivation — determine who reaches recovery
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, highly marginalized and non-representative sample, qualitative methodology limits generalizability, LLM-assisted coding introduces novel methodological uncertainty, single source of narratives (YouTube series)

ideas.title: Most Pokémon packs and Labubu blind boxes don't tell you your odds of a rare pull
ideas.beat: internet culture / kids and gambling-like products
ideas.angle: Researchers checked 50 trading card packs and blind boxes. 80% gave no odds at all, and not one let a buyer work out the chance of getting a specific card. That matters for products sold to kids with no age limit.
ideas.why_now: Online 13 days (verified). The Labubu and Pokémon card frenzies keep these products in the news.
ideas.is_it_real: The sample is small (50 packs) and all from Hong Kong, so the US shelf may differ. The study describes packaging and measures no harm to kids. The idea that this may break consumer law is the authors' argument, not a ruling. Add the caveat in a clause.

studies.headline: 80% of physical trading card packs reveal nothing about your odds of getting a rare card — and that may be illegal
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, WEIRD sample (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic)

ideas.title: Is it real? Going vegan is a red flag for an eating disorder
ideas.beat: viral health and wellness claims / the body
ideas.angle: The claim that plant-based eating is often cover for disordered eating gets repeated by clinicians, parents and online. Pooled across 24 studies, vegetarians and vegans showed no more eating-disorder symptoms than omnivores, and in more-female adult samples they showed slightly fewer. Use it as the receipt and explain what the evidence can and can't say about the people who use veganism as cover.
ideas.why_now: Not on this week's trend list. It's an evergreen claim that keeps resurfacing, and tfm has no age limit (online 110 days).
ideas.is_it_real: It's a meta-analysis of 24 cross-sectional studies and 25,223 people. The overall difference was near zero (SMD 0.07), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 80%). All the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so the study can't say whether people with eating disorders later adopt plant-based diets. The 'possibly protective in women' result comes from a subgroup pattern and should be treated as a hint, not a finding. Community samples may not reflect clinical eating-disorder populations, where the concern began.

studies.headline: Vegetarian and vegan diets are not linked to higher eating disorder symptoms — and in women, they may be associated with fewer
studies.caveats: observational design, cross-sectional studies only (all 24 included studies), self-reported outcomes, short follow-up, high heterogeneity (I²=80.3%), WEIRD sample

ideas.title: ADHD and addiction: about one in five people in substance use treatment has ADHD, and the rate depends on sex and substance
ideas.angle: An evergreen page on ADHD and substance use for women. The pooled rate is 22% across 84 studies. It is highest among people using cannabis (33%) and benzodiazepines (33%, both sexes) and lowest among women using cocaine (5%). This is the first sex-by-substance breakdown, useful for a 'why ADHD and self-medication go together' explainer.
ideas.why_now: Online 107 days, too old to pitch, but steady search demand. The site launches 2026-11-23 and needs foundational pages.
ideas.is_it_real: It's a meta-analysis of 84 studies and 34,036 adults in treatment and support services, so it doesn't represent the general population. Heterogeneity is significant, and settings include prisons. ADHD screening methods varied. It shows co-occurrence, not that ADHD causes substance use.

studies.headline: One in five people in substance use treatment has ADHD — and the rate varies sharply by sex and drug of choice
studies.caveats: observational design, significant heterogeneity across studies, self-reported outcomes likely in many included studies, WEIRD sample (studies conducted in Western healthcare and prison settings), secondary analysis

ideas.title: Why so many women self-diagnose ADHD: 'good girl' expectations hid it for years
ideas.angle: Supporting evidence for an evergreen page on ADHD self-diagnosis and masking in women. Young women describe how pressure to be accomplished and compliant hid their struggles, why self-diagnosis felt validating, and why formal assessment felt out of reach.
ideas.why_now: Online 20 days, but the value is evergreen. 'Self-diagnosed ADHD' is a steady search, and the site launches 2026-11-23.
ideas.is_it_real: Thin. These are interviews with 15 Swedish women aged 18–25, analyzed qualitatively. It shows how they describe their experience, not how common it is or whether their self-diagnoses are accurate. Use it as color beside stronger prevalence and diagnosis-gap data, not as the backbone.

studies.headline: Young women self-diagnosing with ADHD say 'good girl' expectations hid their struggles for years — and formal diagnosis felt out of reach
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, WEIRD sample (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic), qualitative design limits generalizability

ideas.title: Is it real? Give workers more autonomy and they won't burn out under a heavy load
ideas.angle: Managers are told that flexibility, autonomy and support 'buffer' an impossible workload. A machine-learning study of 100,000 German workers found that each resource helps on its own, but none of them cancels out the harm of heavy demands. The honest answer to 'is it real?' is 'half': perks are good, and they don't make an overload safe.
ideas.why_now: Burnout and return-to-office debates come back every quarter. This is the largest test yet of the job demands-resources 'buffer' idea that sits under most workplace wellness programs. No age limit applies to tfm.
ideas.is_it_real: Moderate. The sample is large and quota-representative (n=100,000), but the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, from one country. The study did not find that autonomy is useless. Its main effect still predicts less burnout. What failed is the interaction: autonomy didn't specifically soften the damage of high demands. The digest's headline, 'the biggest idea in burnout research might be wrong', overstates it. Say 'linked to', and don't say resources do nothing.

studies.headline: A massive workplace study finds that job stress and autonomy don't interact the way burnout theory predicts
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-country sample (Germany), cross-sectional design implied

ideas.title: Fifteen of the top empathy scientists say 'empathy' is really 11 different things, and that's why the research keeps contradicting itself
ideas.angle: An ideas or explainer piece. Is empathy a virtue, a weakness, or something that burns you out? Researchers including Jamil Zaki and Jean Decety say the field has been measuring different things under one word: vicarious feeling, compassion, perspective-taking, emotional contagion and more. Untangling them explains why 'empathy' studies seem to say opposite things, and why public fights about empathy talk past each other.
ideas.why_now: Online 30 days, so inside the pitch window, and not widely covered. 'Empathy' is a live culture-war word: tech and political figures have called it a weakness, and the 'toxic empathy' and 'empath' talk keeps going. The pitch agents must confirm that this debate is still current before leaning on it.
ideas.is_it_real: Thin as evidence and solid as authority. It is a consensus and terminology paper with no new data, written by a small, Western group of senior scholars. The story is that the experts agree on a fix, not that a finding emerged. Frans de Waal, who died in 2024, is listed as an author, which suggests the paper took years. Confirm the author list and dates. It can't say whether empathy is good or bad, only that the word hides several distinct things.
ideas.other_peg: Ongoing public argument over whether empathy is a weakness ('toxic empathy', tech-figure comments); pitch agents to verify a current instance

studies.headline: Fifteen leading empathy researchers agree: we need to stop using the word 'empathy' so loosely
studies.caveats: no empirical data collected, consensus/expert opinion paper, WEIRD sample of scholars

ideas.title: By the time a new drug's serious allergic-type side effects reach its label, it has typically been dispensed more than a million times
ideas.angle: FDA's own researchers tracked 339 drugs approved 2002–2014 for a median of 13 years. They found 5,161 safety issues added to labels after approval, led by anaphylaxis, angioedema and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The story isn't that the FDA misses things. It's the honest math of rare harms: a reaction that hits 1 in 10,000 people can't show up in trials of a few thousand, so patients on a new drug are part of its safety testing. What should a patient ask before taking a drug that's only a year or two old?
ideas.why_now: FDA leadership is pushing to speed approvals (for example the 2025 national priority voucher program) while postmarketing surveillance has lost staff. A study by FDA's own scientists on how long label changes lag gives that debate a number.
ideas.is_it_real: A large, descriptive analysis by FDA authors using postmarketing data, so it is credible on what got added to labels and when. Caveats: the 'more than a million prescriptions' figure is a mean for outpatient drugs, so blockbusters pull it up. A label change is not the date FDA first spotted the signal. Some post-approval label additions are expected by design. The online date is unverified; the pitch agents must confirm it's within 30 days.

studies.headline: By the time a new drug's hidden side effects get added to its label, over a million prescriptions have already been filled
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

ideas.title: There are now several pills for breast cancer that outsmarts hormone therapy, and getting one depends on a blood test many patients don't know to ask for
ideas.angle: ESR1 mutations usually develop during hormone therapy for metastatic ER+ breast cancer and quietly cause resistance. Camizestrant (approved in the US, EU, UK, Japan and elsewhere) and vepdegestrant (FDA-approved May 2026, a PROTAC that destroys the estrogen receptor instead of blocking it) join earlier ESR1-targeted pills. All of them require finding the mutation, usually by repeat liquid biopsy. Camizestrant's trial also tested switching drugs when the mutation shows up in blood, before scans show growth: a new and debated way to treat. A patient-facing explainer on what to ask your oncologist.
ideas.why_now: Two approvals in 2026 plus the end of Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The camizestrant review is online 30 days (verified).
ideas.is_it_real: Both papers are regulatory-milestone summaries in the journal Drugs, not new trial data, and the camizestrant piece had manufacturer input (AstraZeneca). The trial results behind them are real, but the benefit is in progression-free survival. The pitch agents must check the overall-survival data and whether switching early on a blood test is proven to help patients live longer, or only delays progression on scans.

studies.headline: New oral pill targets a drug-resistance mutation that defeats standard breast cancer hormone therapy
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, industry funding [AstraZeneca — manufacturer had opportunity to comment on article]

studies.headline: A first-of-its-kind cancer drug that destroys — rather than blocks — estrogen receptors just won FDA approval
studies.caveats: secondary analysis

ideas.title: The fight over a 1956 radiation panel is back, and it is shaping how the US rewrites its radiation safety rules
ideas.beat: history, food, the Midwest and internet culture
ideas.angle: A science-history and policy story. A new analysis of unpublished 1956 NAS BEAR I Genetics Panel reports argues that a panelist removed conflicting estimates to manufacture consensus, and that the mouse mutation data behind the 'linear no-threshold' model were falsified. LNT still underpins radiation limits for medical imaging, nuclear workers and cleanup. The story is the fight: who is making this case, what historians and radiation epidemiologists say back, and what's at stake if regulators loosen limits on the strength of it.
ideas.why_now: Online 54 days (verified), so a second peg is required. The administration has ordered the NRC to overhaul its rules and reconsider LNT, with a deadline around now.
ideas.is_it_real: This is archival historical argument, not new exposure data, and the 'falsified data' charge is the authors' interpretation. It echoes a long-running, contested critique of the BEAR panel (associated with toxicologist Edward Calabrese; confirm the authors). Health Physics is a radiation-protection society journal. Large modern cohorts (A-bomb survivors, nuclear workers, CT-scanned children) are often cited as supporting low-dose risk independent of 1956. The pitch must present this as a dispute, not a verdict.
ideas.other_peg: The May 2025 executive order directing the NRC to revise its regulations and reconsider the linear no-threshold model and ALARA, with an 18-month deadline that falls around November 2026. Pitch agents must confirm the rulemaking's current status.

studies.headline: The 1956 science that set radiation safety rules for the world may have been built on falsified data and suppressed dissent
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

ideas.title: Safety limits built one chemical at a time are missing real exposures, several recent studies suggest
ideas.angle: An explainer on how chemical safety rules are built and where they fail. A European biomonitoring study finds some children exceed safety margins for neurotoxic pesticides only when the chemicals are assessed together, as they occur in the body. A US analysis of nearly 2 million water records finds PFAS limits exceeded for 37 to 81 million people, and many older tests couldn't even detect levels at the legal limit. Workers exposed to methyl methacrylate show DNA damage at doses below occupational limits. Firefighters carry new PFAS that standard panels don't look for. The common thread: what regulators test for is not what people are exposed to.
ideas.why_now: The pesticide-mixture study is online 35 days (verified), so it can be the 'latest'. US PFAS drinking-water limits and compliance deadlines are being revised.
ideas.is_it_real: Each study is limited. The pesticide paper's abstract was truncated before the share of children over threshold was reported, and its intakes are modelled by reverse dosimetry from urine. The PFAS analysis depends on self-reported utility data and gives a wide range of people affected. The methyl methacrylate study is one Chinese plant with 45 exposed workers. The firefighter study has 33 people. Together they make a credible point about blind spots; none of them shows harm to health from the gaps.
ideas.other_peg: EPA's 2025 decision to keep PFOA/PFOS drinking-water limits, extend compliance to 2031 and rescind limits for other PFAS. Pitch agents must confirm current status.

studies.headline: Mixing pesticides in the body may push some European children's neurotoxic risk past the safety threshold
studies.caveats: observational design, European cohorts only (generalizability to US populations uncertain), reverse dosimetry introduces modeling assumptions, abstract truncated before full results reported
studies.fact_check_note: Abstract was truncated before complete results for the percentage of individuals below threshold were reported; summary reflects only what was verifiable in the available text.

studies.headline: Up to 81 million Americans may be drinking PFAS-contaminated water — and regulators can't fully see the problem
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, data quality dependent on local government self-reporting

studies.headline: Workers exposed to a common industrial chemical show DNA damage at levels below the legal safety limit
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design

studies.headline: Firefighters carry novel PFAS chemicals in their blood that standard tests don't even look for — and some spike after fighting fires
studies.caveats: small sample (N=33), single-center, short follow-up, observational design

ideas.title: Before the next pandemic: the research audits of COVID science show underpowered trials, models that ignored behavior, and safety signals no one will ever resolve
ideas.angle: Six years on, researchers are grading the evidence that drove pandemic decisions. Of 463 early COVID drug trials, median power was 9%, and a 'significant' result had only about a 31% chance of being real, versus 94% in normal drug development. Standard epidemic models that ignored behavior change underestimated contagiousness and overestimated final infections at the same time. A WHO database review flagged cardiac and neurological signals for COVID antibody drugs that were withdrawn before anyone could follow them up. The feature asks what has to change before the next one.
ideas.why_now: Bird flu is surging in searches (Indiana, mink), and preparedness is back on the table. The epidemic-model study is online 52 days and the trials analysis 72.
ideas.is_it_real: All three are secondary analyses. The 31% figure is a Bayesian estimate built on assumed pre-trial plausibility. The models paper covers only the first US wave (20 locations). The antibody findings are disproportionality signals in spontaneous reports, which can't show causation. This is a critique of methods, not proof that any particular decision was wrong, and the pitch has to resist being read as 'science failed'.
ideas.other_peg: H5N1 bird flu activity (Indiana, mink) driving preparedness coverage

studies.headline: Only 31% of positive COVID-19 drug trial results likely reflected true efficacy — pandemic urgency gutted the science
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, observational design

studies.headline: Standard epidemic models have a hidden double error: they underestimate how contagious a virus is while overestimating how many people it will infect
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

studies.headline: COVID antibody drugs may have had hidden cardiac and neurological risks that the pandemic's pace of change left permanently unexplored
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis

ideas.title: Is it real? Fluoride in US tap water lowers kids' IQ
ideas.angle: The claim driving state fluoridation bans, checked against the biggest US study yet. In 2,514 children from the ECHO cohort, higher prenatal fluoride from public water was linked to lower fluid-cognition scores only above about 675–1,107 µg/L. That overlaps the 700 µg/L US target and is far below the EPA's 4,000 µg/L limit. The effect was 0.67 points per 100 µg/L on a test with a mean of 100. Not IQ, not nothing, and not what either side says.
ideas.why_now: Utah and Florida ended community fluoridation in 2025 and fluoride is a federal health priority. 'Fluoride lowers IQ' is one of the most repeated health claims in politics.
ideas.is_it_real: Observational. Exposure is the public water system's concentration, not what mothers actually drank. The outcome is NIH Toolbox fluid cognition, not IQ (the digest's 'IQ' wording is wrong). The effect per 100 µg/L is small, and the threshold model's range is wide. It is real evidence of an association in US kids at US-relevant levels, and it doesn't settle causation.

studies.headline: Fluoride in US tap water at levels below federal safety limits is associated with lower cognitive scores in children
studies.caveats: observational design, short follow-up

ideas.title: Tourists left antibiotics in the soil of one of Earth's most remote mountaintops, even far from the campsites
ideas.angle: A weird-stat item. On Roraima-tepui, a 'sky island' above the Amazon with no sanitation, researchers found 11 pharmaceuticals including ciprofloxacin, some in zones visitors don't use. Caveat in a clause: resistance genes weren't measured.
ideas.why_now: Online 18 days (verified). It works for this Friday's roundup.
ideas.is_it_real: Soil chemistry from one site. The detections are real, but the antimicrobial-resistance risk is a modelled estimate, not measured resistance.

studies.headline: Tourists are leaving antibiotics behind on one of Earth's most remote mountaintops — and the drugs are spreading beyond the campsites
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center

ideas.title: Ghost kitchens on delivery apps: what they are, and why so many of their food photos look AI-made
ideas.beat: history, food, the Midwest and internet culture
ideas.angle: An evergreen explainer on delivery-only 'dark kitchen' brands, using a Sydney study of 197 brands on UberEats and DoorDash as the receipt. More than 70% of menu items were fried or dessert-type foods, more than 57% of images showed signs of AI enhancement, and a third of brands closed during the study.
ideas.why_now: Ghost kitchens and AI food photos are a steady food-internet search topic, and the study gives a hard number on the AI imagery.
ideas.is_it_real: Exploratory, one city (Sydney), and how 'AI enhancement' was judged needs checking. Good as one data point on an evergreen page, not as a US claim.

studies.headline: Ghost kitchens are flooding food delivery apps with AI-generated images — and more than 70% of their menus is junk food
studies.caveats: observational design, single-city context (Greater Sydney), exploratory analysis

ideas.title: Norovirus GII.17: the strain that took over by dodging immunity, explained before winter season
ideas.angle: An evergreen explainer on the newer GII.17 norovirus strain for people checking outbreaks. Lab work suggests the 2024 variant spread because people's existing immunity didn't recognize it, not because it binds gut cells better. That helps explain why outbreaks can feel 'new'.
ideas.why_now: Norovirus season runs November through April, and strain names surge in searches during outbreaks.
ideas.is_it_real: A lab study (virus-like particles, 75 human sera, one center). Fine as the 'why this strain spread' paragraph on a page sourced mostly from CDC outbreak data. Not a pitch or roundup item.

studies.headline: A norovirus strain swept Europe not by binding better to gut cells — but by dodging existing immunity
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for sera), observational design, single-center

ideas.title: Canada's news coverage helped sell forced drug treatment on evidence that doesn't hold up
ideas.angle: Researchers read 142 Canadian news articles from 2020 to 2025 and found coverage often treated contested or limited evidence as enough to justify involuntary substance-use treatment, while coercive-care laws spread. The story is the gap between how sure the coverage sounded and what the research shows, at a moment when US cities and states are also expanding civil commitment.
ideas.why_now: Online 44 days and the date is verified. Involuntary treatment is moving from talk to practice in Canada and the US, so the question of what evidence supports it has a live policy clock.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a qualitative media analysis of 142 articles. It shows how the coverage framed evidence. It does not measure whether involuntary treatment works. The underlying claim, that the outcome evidence for coerced treatment is weak, is consistent with prior systematic reviews, but the pitch should cite those directly and not lean on this paper for it. The corpus is Canadian only and self-selected.
ideas.other_peg: Implementation of Alberta's Compassionate Intervention Act, and US moves toward civil commitment, including the July 2025 federal executive order on homelessness and New York's 2025 expansion of involuntary commitment criteria. The pitch agents must confirm where each stands now.

studies.headline: Canada's media is helping sell involuntary drug treatment — even though the evidence says it doesn't work
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, limited to Canadian news media, self-selected corpus

ideas.title: A second kissing-bug species in the Southwest has been caught carrying the Chagas parasite
ideas.angle: Surveillance on military bases near the US-Mexico border in California and Arizona found the Chagas parasite in 9% of Paratriatoma hirsuta bugs, the first confirmation in wild-caught insects of this species, and in 7% of the better-known Triatoma rubida. Kissing bugs are a recurring viral scare, so a short, accurate item is useful.
ideas.why_now: Online 18 days with a verified date. Kissing-bug posts come back every year as viral fear content.
ideas.is_it_real: 83 insects collected from wood rat nests. This shows the parasite is present in the bugs. It does not show human infections. US-acquired Chagas is rare, and most US cases were acquired abroad. Put that in a clause.

studies.journal: The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene
studies.headline: A kissing-bug species never before linked to Chagas disease is now confirmed carrying the parasite near U.S. military bases on the Mexico border
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-region (U.S.-Mexico border)

ideas.title: ADHD and having kids: adults with ADHD become parents earlier but less often, and partnership explains most of the gap
ideas.angle: An evergreen page on ADHD and parenthood. In 759,430 Finns, people with ADHD were more likely to have a first child in their late teens and early twenties and less likely between 24 and 38. Once partnership status was accounted for, the overall negative link reversed.
ideas.why_now: Too old to pitch (124 days), but strong evidence for a steady-search topic on the women's ADHD site, which launches 2026-11-23. Fertility rate is also trending this week.
ideas.is_it_real: A very large population-register cohort, but observational and from one country (Finland). ADHD was identified from health records and prescriptions, so it captures diagnosed ADHD only. The summary does not say whether results were split by sex, so check before writing a women-specific claim.

studies.journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
studies.headline: People with ADHD become parents earlier but are ultimately less likely to have children at all
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (Finland), secondary analysis

ideas.title: Traveling abroad with ADHD medication: what to check before you fly
ideas.beat: women's health and the mind: ADHD
ideas.angle: An evergreen service page for the Women's ADHD site. Stimulants count as controlled substances in many countries, so the page covers paperwork, how long a supply you can carry, prescription letters, layovers and keeping routines on long trips. The Journal of Travel Medicine commentary gives it a clinical source.
ideas.why_now: The site launches 2026-11-23, right before holiday travel. People search 'traveling with adhd medication' every year, and the page doesn't depend on news timing.
ideas.is_it_real: This is an expert commentary from the University of Galway, not a study. It has no data, no participants and no abstract, and the digest says its summary is based only on the title and study type. It's fine as one clinical source on a practical page. Each country's medication rules have to be checked against official government or embassy sources, not taken from this paper.
ideas.other_peg: Holiday travel season; Women's ADHD site launch 2026-11-23

studies.headline: Traveling abroad with ADHD raises hidden logistical and legal hurdles that most travel medicine clinics aren't prepared for
studies.caveats: observational design, small sample (N<100), self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis
studies.fact_check_note: No abstract data were available beyond the title and author affiliations; summary and caveats are based on the study type and title only. Journalists should verify specific claims against the full text.

ideas.title: Microdosing for ADHD: what the evidence actually says
ideas.beat: women's health and the mind: ADHD
ideas.angle: An evergreen explainer for the Women's ADHD site. People search this often, and the honest answer is that there's very little evidence. This review finds the clinical data are mostly small ketamine studies in adults, while data on LSD and psilocybin are scarce and mostly observational. The page should lead with that gap, not with 'promising'.
ideas.why_now: Interest in microdosing and psychedelics for ADHD is steady, and the site needs pages that hold up before it launches 2026-11-23. Age doesn't matter for a brief.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a narrative review from Milano-Bicocca of mostly small, observational or preclinical work, and much of it is about autism rather than ADHD. The digest calls the findings 'promising', but the underlying studies don't support that. The brief room should look for any placebo-controlled microdosing trials in adult ADHD and give them more weight than this review. Don't present it as evidence that psychedelics work.

studies.headline: Could psychedelics treat autism and ADHD? Early evidence is promising — and complicated
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, secondary analysis

ideas.title: How does salmonella get into lettuce and other produce? The irrigation-water problem behind recalls
ideas.angle: A food safety explainer for Recall Register on why fresh produce keeps being recalled for salmonella. Surface water from creeks, ponds and rivers used for irrigation regularly carries the bacteria. Scientists still can't reliably predict when it does, and the review says US rules have gaps here.
ideas.why_now: Recall weeks keep sending readers to Recall Register (this week: ready-to-eat meat and Family Farmstead cheese). A standing produce-and-salmonella explainer gives recall posts something to link to.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a literature review from the University of Georgia in the Journal of Food Protection, with no new data. It's solid as a background source on contamination pathways. Its illness and death figures are global estimates, so US numbers should come from CDC. The online date isn't verified, which doesn't matter for an evergreen page.
ideas.seed_keyword: how does salmonella get on produce

studies.headline: The irrigation water feeding your salad may harbor Salmonella — and scientists still can't reliably predict when or why
studies.caveats: secondary analysis

ideas.title: Is it real? The 'billions of live bacteria' on your probiotic label
ideas.angle: Test the number on the bottle. A systematic review of how probiotics are manufactured finds that fermentation, drying, packaging and storage each kill off bacteria, with each drying stage typically losing 90% to 99.9% of them. So the CFU count on the label may not be the live dose that reaches your gut. The study is the receipt; the post checks how labels are actually worded and what independent product tests found.
ideas.why_now: Supplement formats are a live 'is it real?' topic this week: Trend Desk has 'Supplement strips are replacing gummies' as a tfm idea. This is the companion question about whether what's printed on the bottle is what you swallow. The editor could fold it into that post instead of running a separate one.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a review of the manufacturing literature, not a test of products on store shelves. It shows where bacteria die during production, not that any given brand falls short of its label. Manufacturers may add extra bacteria to make up for losses, and labels may state counts at the time of manufacture or at expiration. Both have to be checked, not assumed. 'Mostly dead by the time you swallow it' overstates what the paper shows.
ideas.other_peg: Trend Desk tfm idea on supplement strips vs gummies

studies.headline: Probiotic pills may lose billions of bacteria before they ever reach your gut
studies.caveats: review article (no primary data), single-institution authors

ideas.title: Families are being sold 40 Hz light headsets, hyperbaric oxygen and companion robots for memory. The evidence mostly stops at 'people liked it'
ideas.beat: aging, body and metabolism; health tech
ideas.angle: Brain-health gadgets and clinic treatments are sold to worried older adults and their adult children. Four new evidence pieces show how little is behind them. The best-designed 40 Hz light trial missed its main brain-activity outcome. The whole human evidence base for 40 Hz is eight small studies. Hyperbaric oxygen for people over 50 rests on 502 people followed for 12 weeks at most. Robot and VR dementia tools have only been tested for feasibility.
ideas.why_now: All four were published in the last three weeks (12 to 22 days ago), and the lead review is 12 days old. 40 Hz devices and hyperbaric 'longevity' sessions are on sale to consumers now. The searches 'napping and dementia' and 'slow cognitive processing' are spiking, which shows how anxious people are about memory.
ideas.is_it_real: Moderate as a pattern, but every piece is small. The 40 Hz review covers eight heterogeneous studies; its pooled brain-volume result was exploratory and fell apart in sensitivity analysis, and two of its authors co-wrote included studies. The 40 Hz pilot had 33 people, and its memory signals came from unadjusted secondary analyses. The hyperbaric review is not negative: two small studies in healthy older adults reported cognitive gains, so the honest line is 'thin and short', not 'debunked'. The robot/VR review is a thematic synthesis with no effect sizes. Absence of proof is not proof of no effect. The pitch should not name trial readout dates or company claims it hasn't verified.

studies.headline: Robots, VR and smart apps for Alzheimer's care: engaging in the short term, unproven over the long haul
studies.caveats: Systematic review of mostly small feasibility studies with no long-term effectiveness data; only four databases searched; findings synthesized thematically rather than pooled statistically, so no effect size can be quoted; included study populations and technologies were highly heterogeneous.

studies.headline: 40 Hz light and sound therapy for Alzheimer's: promising brain scans, but no proven memory benefit yet
studies.caveats: Systematic review of only eight small, heterogeneous studies with non-overlapping outcomes; biomarker evidence came from a single uncontrolled study; the pooled meta-analysis was explicitly labeled exploratory and was not robust to sensitivity analysis; two review authors co-wrote three of the included EEG studies, though they recused themselves from assessing their own work.

studies.headline: A 4-week trial of '40 Hz' light therapy failed to change brain activity in healthy older adults
studies.caveats: Pilot trial with only 33 participants (29 analyzed), single center, cognitively normal volunteers who may not reflect people with memory impairment, short four-week intervention with no long-term follow-up, and the positive memory signals came from unadjusted exploratory analyses.

studies.headline: Hyperbaric oxygen chambers are marketed as anti-aging therapy. Here's what the evidence actually shows.
studies.caveats: Systematic review of only seven heterogeneous studies with 502 total participants; protocols varied widely in pressure, duration and frequency; mostly moderate methodological quality; short follow-up leaves durability unknown; no pooled meta-analysis.

ideas.title: The updated US migraine-prevention guideline: which daily drug fits whom, including people with obesity, high blood pressure or medication overuse
ideas.angle: The American Academy of Neurology and the American Headache Society have reissued their guidance on preventive migraine drugs. It covers when to start one, how to choose, how to tell whether it's working, and when to stop, with specific advice for patients with obesity, hypertension, fibromyalgia or medication overuse. Migraine affects women about three times as often as men, so this is a 'what changed and what to ask your neurologist' service piece.
ideas.why_now: Online 12 days and not widely covered. A national guideline from the two main specialty societies is its own news peg.
ideas.is_it_real: This is a clinical practice guideline built on a systematic review of evidence through June 2024, not new research. The abstract doesn't say which drugs were recommended or how strongly.
